Week 9 Summary — Critical Perspectives on Predictive Policing

1. Opening Question
	•	Before asking HOW to build predictive policing systems, ask: SHOULD we?
	•	A statistically "good" model can still be socially harmful.
	•	Both technical skills AND critical evaluation are essential for ethical data science.

2. The Sales Pitch vs Reality
	•	Vendor claims: Efficiency, objectivity, proactivity, data-driven.
	•	Critical assumptions that often fail:
	•	Crime data accurately reflects crime (it doesn't).
	•	Past patterns predict future crime (they might just predict policing).
	•	We can separate "good" from "bad" data (we often can't).
	•	Technical solutions can fix social problems (they can't).

3. The Dirty Data Problem
	•	Traditional definition: Missing data, incorrect data, non-standardized formats.
	•	Extended definition (Richardson et al. 2019): Data derived from or influenced by corrupt, biased, and unlawful practices.
	•	Forms of dirty data:
	•	Fabricated/Manipulated: False arrests, downgraded crime classifications ("juking the stats").
	•	Systematically Biased: Over-policing certain communities, under-policing white-collar crime.
	•	Missing/Incomplete: Unreported crimes, ignored complaints.
	•	Proxy Problems: Arrests ≠ crimes committed; calls for service ≠ actual need.

4. Case Studies
	•	Baltimore: 14,000+ serious assaults misrecorded, Gun Trace Task Force corruption, officers robbing residents and planting evidence.
	•	NYPD CompStat: Pressure led to stat manipulation, downgrading serious crimes, persuading victims not to file reports.
	•	The Feedback Loop: Algorithm predicts crime in area X → Police sent to X → More arrests in X → Algorithm "confirmed" → Cycle intensifies.

5. Why "Cleaning" Data Isn't Enough
	•	Crime reports reflect police decisions (what to investigate, classify, document).
	•	Calls for service reflect community bias (e.g., gentrification → increased 311 calls).
	•	Crime data is always: Socially constructed, selectively enforced, organizationally filtered, politically shaped.
	•	Crime data doesn't reveal "crime" — it reveals policing patterns.

6. Consequences and Harms
	•	False Positives (predicted high risk, no crime): Increased harassment, trauma, broken trust, economic harm.
	•	False Negatives (predicted low risk, crime occurs): Inadequate police response, unequal protection.
	•	Both types disproportionately affect Black/Brown communities.

7. Consent Decrees: Limitations
	•	Typical reforms: Training, oversight, use-of-force policies, data collection.
	•	What they DON'T address: Historical dirty data, ongoing use in algorithms, vendor accountability, public transparency.

8. Framework for Critical Evaluation
	•	Data Provenance: What time period? Civil rights investigations during that period? Evidence data is accurate?
	•	Variable Selection: What variables used? How might each embed bias? What's excluded?
	•	Validation: How is accuracy measured? Error rates by neighborhood? Who experiences false positives vs negatives?
	•	Deployment: How do predictions translate to action? What discretion do officers have?
	•	Transparency & Accountability: Is methodology public? Can individuals challenge predictions?
	•	Alternatives: What non-punitive interventions were considered?

9. Technical Foundations: Local Spatial Autocorrelation
	•	Global Moran's I: One value for entire study area — "Is there clustering overall?"
	•	Local Moran's I (LISA): One value per location — "Where are the clusters?"
	•	Four cluster types:
	•	High-High: Hotspot (high crime surrounded by high crime).
	•	Low-Low: Coldspot (low crime surrounded by low crime).
	•	High-Low: Outlier (isolated high).
	•	Low-High: Outlier (isolated low).
	•	Statistical significance: Use permutation test (999 permutations) to identify real clusters.

10. Spatial Weights Matrix
	•	Define "neighbors" using: Contiguity (Queen/Rook), Distance threshold, K-nearest neighbors.
	•	Row standardization (style = "W"): Each row sums to 1, makes cells comparable regardless of number of neighbors.

11. Count Regression: Poisson and Negative Binomial
	•	Poisson Regression: For count data; assumes variance = mean.
	•	Overdispersion: When variance > mean (common in crime data).
	•	Check: Dispersion = Residual Deviance / Degrees of Freedom; if > 1.5, use Negative Binomial.
	•	Negative Binomial: Adds dispersion parameter; Var(Y) = μ + αμ²; accommodates overdispersion.
	•	Compare models using AIC (lower is better).

12. Key Takeaways
	•	Before asking "Does it work?", ask "Should we be doing this at all?"
	•	A system that accurately predicts where over-policing will occur is "accurate" but not necessarily just.
	•	Technical fixes cannot solve fundamentally social problems.
	•	Both technical competence and ethical reflection are essential.
